``` {.julia .cell-code}
temp_ = @chain ponds begin @filter(hydro == "temporary") end

```

::: {.callout-note .exercise}
## Your turn 8.1 — Does hydroperiod affect body size?

Compare `body_size` between permanent and temporary ponds with a Welch t test. Pass
its p-value to `check("8.1", ...)`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Reuse `perm` and `temp_` from the block above. `pvalue(test)` extracts the p-value.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
t_body = UnequalVarianceTTest(perm.body_size, temp_.body_size)
pvalue(t_body)
```

::: {#answer-8-1 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
```
0.10269215805061378
```
:::
:::



::: {#answer-8-1-check .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
check("8.1", pvalue(t_body))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
✓ Correct!
```
:::
:::



p ≈ 0.10: no evidence of a difference. Here we can go further than usual, because in
the simulation hydroperiod really has no effect on body size. With real data, a
non-significant test does not show that there is no effect — only that the data
cannot tell.
:::
:::

``` {.julia .cell-code}
        Normal(0, 1)) |> pvalue,
    correlation = CorrelationTest(ponds.canopy, ponds.body_size) |> pvalue,
)
```

## Diagnostics {#sec-diagnostics}

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
res = residuals(m3)
fit_ = predict(m3)

fig = Figure(size = (860, 350))

ax1 = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Fitted values", ylabel = "Residuals",
           title = "(a) Residuals vs fitted")
scatter!(ax1, fit_, res, color = (:steelblue, 0.6))
hlines!(ax1, 0, color = :grey40, linestyle = :dash)

ax2 = Axis(fig[1, 2], xlabel = "Theoretical quantiles", ylabel = "Sample quantiles",
           title = "(b) QQ plot")
# NOTE: Makie exports `qqnorm` as a plot recipe, so the quantiles are
# computed explicitly here rather than taken from a helper.
n = length(res)
theoretical = quantile.(Normal(0, 1), ((1:n) .- 0.5) ./ n)
scatter!(ax2, theoretical, sort(res), color = (:darkorange, 0.6))
ablines!(ax2, 0, std(res), color = :grey40, linestyle = :dash)

ax3 = Axis(fig[1, 3], xlabel = "Residuals", ylabel = "Frequency",
           title = "(c) Distribution")
hist!(ax3, res, bins = 20, color = (:seagreen, 0.7))

fig
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## A real gap

R has `plot(model)`, which returns the four diagnostic plots at once, and
`performance::check_model()`, which goes much further. Julia has no consolidated
equivalent; the diagnostics above are assembled by hand. This is a genuine gap, and
exactly the kind of thing a community package would fix well.
:::

## Mixed models {#sec-mixed-models}

`MixedModels.jl` [@mixedmodelsjl] is maintained by Douglas Bates, first author of
`lme4` [@bates2015lme4], and uses the same formula notation — including `(1 | group)`.

On performance: comparisons between the two depend heavily on the model, the size of
the data and the random-effects structure, and I know of no published benchmark I can
cite here. If fitting time matters for your problem, measure it on your own case.

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
mm1 = fit(MixedModel,
          @formula(body_size ~ temp_c + canopy + (1 | region)),
          ponds)
```

## Your turn 8.6 — A random intercept for region

Fit a mixed model of `body_size` on `temp_c` with a random intercept for `region` and
pass its fixed effects to `check("8.6", ...)`. Then look at `VarCorr` of your model:
how much variation does region account for?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint

Same structure as `mm1`, with a shorter formula. `fixef(mm)` returns the fixed
effects.
:::

::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
mm_temp = fit(MixedModel, @formula(body_size ~ temp_c + (1 | region)), ponds;
              progress = false)
fixef(mm_temp)
```

::: {#answer-8-6 .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1}
```
2-element Vector{Float64}:
 13.183682687070245
  0.9217361109462586
```
:::
:::



::: {.cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code}
check("8.6", fixef(mm_temp))
VarCorr(mm_temp)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
✓ Correct!
```
:::

::: {#answer-8-6-check .cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=1}
|          | Column      |  Variance | Std.Dev |
|:-------- |:----------- | ---------:| -------:|
| region   | (Intercept) |   0.00000 | 0.00000 |
| Residual |             |   5.81124 | 2.41065 |

:::
:::



The region variance is estimated as exactly zero — a *singular* fit. The simulation
has no region effect on body size, and three regions give very little information
about a variance anyway. With a zero variance, the mixed model reduces to
`lm(@formula(body_size ~ temp_c), ponds)`: compare the coefficients.
